overview.title: Choosing the epoch count and training the final model
overview.section: 4.3 Predicting house prices: A regression example
overview.subsection: 4.3.4 Validating your approach using K-fold validation
overview.main_topic: Reading the zoomed validation-MAE curve (figure 4.11) to pick ~130 epochs, then retraining a fresh model on all 480 training samples and evaluating it once on the test set
overview.central_idea: With the first 10 epochs removed, the averaged K-fold curve shows validation MAE no longer improving meaningfully after 120-140 epochs. The book treats training beyond that as overfitting. Once hyperparameters are settled, a new model is trained on the full training set with the chosen settings (130 epochs) and evaluated on the untouched test data.
overview.importance: This page completes the model-selection loop: validation (here K-fold) chooses the hyperparameters, a final fit uses all available training data, and the test set is used exactly once for an unbiased estimate. The same workflow returns in chapters 5, 6 and 18.

summary:
The page opens with the last four lines of **listing 4.32** (begun on p.156). `plt.plot(epochs, truncated_mae_history)` draws the averaged validation MAE without its first 10 points, labeled "Epochs" / "Validation MAE". The result is **figure 4.11**. Now that the y-axis only has to span about 0.28-0.41, the curve shows real structure. It falls from about 0.41 at epoch 10 to about 0.30 by roughly epoch 40-50, then wanders in a noisy band between about 0.285 and 0.315 up to epoch 200.

The authors read this plot as: **validation MAE stops improving significantly after 120-140 epochs**. They add that this count *includes* the 10 omitted epochs, because the x-axis of listing 4.32 was offset to keep original epoch numbering. Beyond that point, *you start overfitting*: further training fits the training folds better without helping the held-out fold.

The second paragraph describes the end of the workflow. Once you have finished tuning the number of epochs and any other parameters (the book suggests the size of the intermediate layers), you **train a final production model on all of the training data** with the best parameters, and only then look at its **test** performance. The K-fold models were each trained on only 360 samples and are discarded. The final model gets all 480.

**Listing 4.33** does exactly this. `get_model()` returns a fresh, compiled model (callout). `model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=130, batch_size=16, verbose=0)` trains it on the entirety of the data (callout), using 130 epochs, the middle of the 120-140 range, and the same batch size as the K-fold runs. `model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)` returns the loss (MSE) and the metric (MAE), which are unpacked into `test_mean_squared_error` and `test_mean_absolute_error`. The result, an MAE of about \$31,000, is printed on p.158.

paragraphs.excerpt: According to this plot (see figure 4.11), validation MAE stops improving significantly
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure 4.11 shows validation MAE stops improving significantly after 120-140 epochs. That count includes the 10 omitted epochs. After that point the model starts overfitting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors pick a range rather than a single minimum because the curve is noisy: individual epochs bounce by ±0.01-0.015 around the plateau. 'Includes the 10 epochs we omitted' is a reminder that listing 4.32 plotted the truncated list at x = 10..199, so the x-axis values are true epoch counts and do not need correcting. 'Overfitting' here means that more training no longer reduces error on unseen data and begins to tailor the model to its training folds.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This choice sets epochs=130 in listing 4.33. Choosing too few epochs underfits, and choosing too many wastes compute and slightly overfits.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Early-stopping point selected by eye on a cross-validated learning curve. Chapter 7 automates this with the EarlyStopping callback (p.233).

terminology.meaning: Training performance keeps improving while validation performance stalls or degrades.
The trend flattens. Remaining changes are within the epoch-to-epoch noise.

connections: p.138: on IMDb, validation metrics peaked at epoch 4, a much clearer overfitting signal than here.
p.233: EarlyStopping stops training automatically when the monitored metric stops improving.

paragraphs.excerpt: Once you’re finished tuning other parameters of the model (in addition to the number
paragraphs.what_it_says: After tuning the epoch count and any other parameters, such as intermediate layer size, you train a final production model on all of the training data with the best parameters, and then check its performance on the test data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: K-fold validation is a measuring device, not a source of the final model. Its four models each saw only 3/4 of the training data. Once it has told you which configuration is best, you build that configuration again and train it on all 480 samples, because more data generally gives a better model. The test set has not been touched by any of this tuning, so evaluating on it gives an honest estimate of real-world performance.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This separates three roles: training data fits weights, validation data chooses hyperparameters, and test data produces the final report. Mixing them, for example by tuning on test scores, makes the reported performance over-optimistic (see chapter 6, p.207, on information leaks).

terminology.meaning: The model you actually deploy, trained with the chosen hyperparameters on all available training data.
The hidden Dense(64) layers of get_model(); their size is another hyperparameter.

connections: p.568: chapter 18 likewise retrains final models on the totality of the training data after a hyperparameter search.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: The point beyond which further training improves fit on training data but no longer on unseen data.
concepts.intuition: After about 130 epochs the network is mostly learning the idiosyncrasies of its 360 training districts.
concepts.technical: Diagnosed here from the averaged validation MAE of 4-fold cross-validation. The curve's improving trend ends around epoch 120-140.
concepts.significance: It determines the training length of the final model.
concepts.example: Figure 4.11: no sustained improvement after roughly epoch 120-140 (book's reading).
concepts.misconception: Overfitting does not always show up as a sharp U-shaped curve. On small, noisy datasets it can be a plateau with a slight drift.

concepts.name: K-fold validation for hyperparameter selection
concepts.definition: Using the average validation score over K folds to choose hyperparameters such as the number of epochs.
concepts.intuition: Four noisy opinions averaged into one reliable one.
concepts.technical: The averaged per-epoch curve (listing 4.30) is inspected, and the epoch where its improvement stops is selected.
concepts.significance: It gives a reliable choice with only 480 training samples.
concepts.example: The choice of 130 epochs in listing 4.33 comes from this procedure.
concepts.misconception: You do not average or ensemble the K fold models for deployment in this workflow. You retrain one model on all the data.

concepts.name: Retraining the final model on all training data
concepts.definition: After hyperparameters are fixed, a fresh model is trained on the full training set (no validation hold-out) and evaluated on the test set.
concepts.intuition: The validation split was scaffolding. Once you know the recipe, you cook with all the ingredients.
concepts.technical: listing 4.33: get_model(); fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=130, batch_size=16); evaluate(x_test, y_test).
concepts.significance: It uses 33% more training data than each K-fold model (480 vs 360 samples).
concepts.example: Test MAE of about \$31,000 is reported on p.158.
concepts.misconception: Training on all the data does not make the epoch count invalid. Strictly, though, a model with more data per epoch takes more gradient steps per epoch (30 batches of 16 instead of 23), so the optimum may shift slightly. (AI note, not in the book.)

concepts.name: Test set
concepts.definition: Held-out data (120 districts here) never used for training or tuning, evaluated once at the end.
concepts.intuition: The final exam you have never seen practice questions from.
concepts.technical: evaluate() returns [loss, metrics...], here [MSE, MAE] on the scaled targets.
concepts.significance: It provides an unbiased estimate of generalization because no decision was based on it.
concepts.misconception: Looking at test scores and then going back to adjust the model turns the test set into a validation set.

code.title: Training the final model
code.original_code:
model = get_model()
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=130, batch_size=16, verbose=0)
test_mean_squared_error, test_mean_absolute_error = model.evaluate(
    x_test, y_test
)
code.what_it_does: Builds a fresh compiled model, trains it for 130 epochs on all 480 training samples, and evaluates it on the 120 test samples.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: 'Gets a fresh, compiled model.' A new instance with new random weights, so nothing from the K-fold runs carries over.

Callout: 'Trains it on the entirety of the data.' Full x_train/y_train, no validation_data, 130 epochs (inside the 120-140 range read from figure 4.11), batch_size=16 as in K-fold, verbose=0 to suppress progress output.
evaluate() returns [loss, mean_absolute_error] because get_model() was compiled with loss='mean_squared_error' and metrics=['mean_absolute_error']. The two values are unpacked into named variables.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: normalized x_train (480, 8), scaled y_train (480,), x_test (120, 8), y_test (120,). Outputs: two floats, test MSE and test MAE, in scaled units (x100,000 for dollars).
code.algorithm: Refit on the full training set with the selected hyperparameters, then a single test evaluation.
code.theory_link: Model selection is done by validation and reporting by test, so the reported test error is unbiased.

deeper.title: Reading figure 4.11 honestly
deeper.body: From the image: the curve starts at about 0.41 at epoch 10, falls below 0.33 by about epoch 25, reaches about 0.30 by epoch 40-50, and then fluctuates roughly between 0.285 and 0.315. Our interpretation (not stated in the book): the plateau begins well before epoch 120, and any upward drift afterward is small relative to the noise. The book's 120-140 is a reasonable conservative choice: enough training to be safely on the plateau, without going all the way to 200 epochs. On a dataset this small, choices anywhere on the plateau give similar test error.

deeper.title: Why retrain instead of reusing a fold model
deeper.body:
1. Each K-fold model trained on 360 of 480 samples (75%).
2. K-fold has answered the question 'how many epochs?'.
3. A model trained on all 480 samples should generalize at least as well, with more data and the same recipe.
4. The test set (120 samples) has never influenced any decision, so evaluating once on it gives a clean estimate.

Beyond the book: an alternative used in practice is to average the predictions of the K fold models (a small ensemble). The book does not do this here.

deeper.title: Validation is a rehearsal, the test is the show
deeper.body: Rehearsals (validation folds) let the director decide the length of each scene (epochs) and the cast size (layer width). On opening night (the test set) the full cast performs once, and the critics' review is the number you report. Re-rehearsing after reading the reviews would make the next review meaningless.

takeaways: Figure 4.11 is the averaged K-fold validation MAE from epoch 10 to 200, with a y-range of about 0.28-0.41.
The book reads it as: no significant improvement after 120-140 epochs (x-values are true epoch counts), and overfitting beyond that.
Other hyperparameters, such as hidden-layer size, can be tuned the same way before the final fit.
The final model is a fresh get_model() trained on all 480 training samples for 130 epochs with batch size 16.
evaluate(x_test, y_test) returns [MSE, MAE] on scaled targets. Test data is used once, at the end.

questions.question: Why do the authors say the 120-140 epoch estimate 'includes the 10 epochs we omitted'?
options: Because the model was retrained for 10 extra epochs
Because listing 4.32 offset the x-axis to start at 10, so plotted x-values are real epoch numbers
Because Keras adds 10 warm-up epochs automatically
Because the first 10 epochs were averaged into epoch 10
questions.answer: Because listing 4.32 offset the x-axis to start at 10, so plotted x-values are real epoch numbers
questions.explanation: epochs = range(10, len(truncated_mae_history) + 10) keeps original numbering, so no correction is needed. There is no retraining, warm-up or merging of epochs.

questions.question: What does each callout in listing 4.33 say, and why does each step matter?
questions.answer: 'Gets a fresh, compiled model' means new random weights, so no K-fold training carries over. 'Trains it on the entirety of the data' means all 480 training samples, with nothing held out, because the hyperparameters are already chosen.
questions.explanation: A fresh model avoids continuing from a fold model's weights. Training on all the data maximizes what the final model learns.

questions.question: Why train a new model on all the training data instead of deploying the best of the four K-fold models?
questions.answer: The fold models each saw only 75% of the training data (360 samples), and K-fold's purpose was to estimate performance and choose hyperparameters. With those fixed, a model trained on all 480 samples should generalize better, and the untouched test set can then measure it fairly.
questions.explanation: This follows the book's instruction to 'train a final production model on all of the training data, with the best parameters, and then look at its performance on the test data.'

questions.question: What does model.evaluate(x_test, y_test) return in listing 4.33?
options: The test loss (MSE) and the test MAE
questions.answer: The test loss (MSE) and the test MAE
questions.explanation: evaluate returns the compiled loss followed by metrics. get_model() used loss='mean_squared_error' and metrics=['mean_absolute_error']. Predictions come from predict() (p.158). Training metrics are not returned by evaluate.

questions.question: Besides the number of epochs, which other parameter does the book suggest tuning before the final fit?
questions.answer: The size of the intermediate layers (the number of units in the hidden Dense layers).
questions.explanation: This is stated explicitly in the second paragraph.

questions.question: Looking at figure 4.11, why might the authors give a range (120-140) rather than the single epoch with the lowest MAE?
questions.answer: The curve is noisy. Epoch-to-epoch fluctuations of about ±0.01-0.015 are as large as any remaining trend, so the single minimum is partly luck. A range around where the trend ends is more robust.
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation of the figure rather than an explicit statement in the book. Picking the noisy minimum would overfit to the validation folds.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, the full chain from listing 4.29 to listing 4.33: what is computed, what is plotted, what is decided, and what is reported?
questions.answer: Per-fold 200-epoch MAE logs are collected, averaged per epoch, plotted with the first 10 epochs dropped, and used to choose about 130 epochs. A fresh model is then trained on all training data and evaluated once on the test set.
questions.explanation: If any link is unclear, revisit p.155-157.
